content: A successful HIV patient monitoring system relies on collaboration and cooperation among various partners within the health sector. This includes HIV programs, which should establish a standardized minimum dataset as the foundation of any national HIV patient monitoring system. This dataset should define the data collected across systems, whether paper-based or transitioning to electronic systems. Facilities with more resources may collect additional data, but standardized tools are critical for supervision, data aggregation, and patient transfers between facilities. The HIV patient monitoring system should be integrated into the national Health Management Information System (HMIS), with standardized and well-defined data elements and indicators. Electronic systems should also be harmonized, and the HMIS should include priority national and global HIV indicators, with the patient monitoring system contributing to many of these indicators (e.g., the number of pregnant women receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART) from antenatal care and HIV clinics). As ART access expands, HIV will become one of several treatable chronic diseases requiring longitudinal patient follow-up. Collaboration between related national programs, such as tuberculosis (TB), maternal, newborn, and child health (MNCH), reproductive and sexual health, and other communicable and chronic diseases, is vital for the success of HIV programs. For example, an HIV-positive pregnant woman can receive antenatal care and HIV care at the same facility. Integrating HIV data into other program records and the HMIS, as well as standardizing HIV indicators across program areas, is essential. Internal institutions can collaborate through technical working groups to provide broader support for improving overall program performance. Patient monitoring requires the involvement of a wide range of staff with overlapping responsibilities, facilitated by task-shifting to lower-level cadres and lay providers. For electronic systems, roles such as maintaining electronic medical records (EMRs) or electronic registers may replace traditional paper-based roles, but staff responsibilities remain consistent. Strengthening human resources for patient monitoring includes training, clinical mentoring, and supervision. They should integrate patient monitoring into clinical mentoring and supervision visits, conduct periodic reviews, assist staff with data analysis and reporting, and provide feedback from previous reports and audits. Specific roles for staff include: Triage workers/receptionists/data clerks: Maintain appointment books, retrieve patient records, and record patient data. ART aides/counselors: Record patient data and provide adherence counseling. Nurses/clinicians: Record patient data, conduct patient reviews, and analyze program reports. Data clerks/secretaries: Organize and manage patient records, transcribe data, and enter data into databases. Community health workers: Initiate HIV testing, monitor adherence, and trace lost patients. Pharmacists: Dispense drugs, manage drug-related toxicity, and provide adherence counseling. Transitioning from paper-based to electronic patient monitoring systems is driven by the increasing difficulty of managing large volumes of data and the need for accurate and reliable data retrieval. This transition may involve various levels of electronic entry, such as EMRs, electronic registers, or electronic reports generated from paper records. A tiered approach allows facilities to adopt electronic systems based on available resources, with the flexibility to transition to higher tiers as infrastructure improves. Improving national and global reporting requires a focus on a few high-quality, well-reported indicators rather than numerous poorly reported ones. Establishing good-quality primary data is the first step, followed by minimizing and harmonizing the number of reportable indicators. Data aggregation should be facilitated at each administrative level, starting at the facility level, with accountability for reported data. HIV case surveillance involves reporting key sentinel events, such as HIV diagnosis, entry into care, ART initiation, and viral suppression, to public health agencies. This system collects individual-level data linked over time, enabling de-duplication of records and monitoring of program effectiveness. Countries should invest in robust and secure data systems, ensuring interoperability and adopting open-source standards. WHO recommends allocating 5–10% of program budgets to strengthen monitoring and evaluation. Ethical principles, such as confidentiality and data security, are fundamental to HIV case surveillance and patient monitoring systems.
